articles.title: NASA Webb Explores Family Tree of Newly Discovered Distant Objects
articles.summary: Since their discovery by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, little red dots (LRDs) have been the subject of great interest to astronomers. Understanding the nature of these extremely distant, compact red sources has been a puzzling scientific endeavor. One popular theory is that little red dots are supermassive black holes known as active […]
articles.content:
Since their discovery by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, little red dots (LRDs) have been the subject of great interest to astronomers. Understanding the nature of these extremely distant, compact red sources has been a puzzling scientific endeavor.

One popular theory is that little red dots are supermassive black holes known as active galactic nuclei, although they display characteristics unlike nearby active galactic nuclei. While they appear abundant at high redshift early in the universe, they rapidly decrease in number at lower redshifts. (The higher the redshift, the greater the distance the light has traveled across the universe.) This perplexing shift in number raises the question: What happens to little red dots as the universe matures?

A team of researchers led by Pierluigi Rinaldi of the University of Arizona’s Steward Observatory, now at the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI) in Baltimore, has built upon their previous research in a new study published on July 29 in The Astrophysical Journal and proposed one pathway LRDs can follow as the universe ages: Though they may look like a unique galaxy population, these dots are affected by observational bias — some features just don’t appear at higher redshifts with current technology.

Image: Saguaro in GOODS-North Field (NIRCam)

Scientists have proposed one pathway little red dots can follow as the universe matures based on their analysis of spiral galaxy WISEA J123635.56+621424.2, nicknamed the “Saguaro.” They suggest little red dots may be a temporary phase of highly active supermassive black holes. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Pierluigi Rinaldi (Steward Observatory); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI)

Their conclusions are based on their analysis of lower-redshift spiral galaxy WISEA J123635.56+621424.2, nicknamed the “Saguaro” for its prominent arms, like the cactus native to the Sonoran Desert in the Southwestern United States. A particularly intriguing feature of this redshift 2 galaxy, which corresponds to approximately 3.3 billion years after the big bang, is its little red dot-like center that is reminiscent of the ruby red fruit produced by the desert plant.

“Everything created in the early universe must evolve into something around us. We have had little idea of what LRDs become, but these results finally show us how to find their progeny,” said co-author George Rieke of the University of Arizona. Previous studies by NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope provided the first hint of the dust-obscured, compact galaxy population in the lower-redshift universe that the Saguaro belongs to, paving the way for NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes’ high-resolution analyses.

“The Saguaro is important because it’s a prototypical little red dot and is one of the few we have found at lower redshift. It can be used to study the pathway of these dots throughout cosmic time,” said Fabio Pacucci of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and a co-author of the study.

Among the thousands of sources Rinaldi looked at across several surveys, the Saguaro was an example of the right place — with one of Webb’s microshutter arrays perfectly framed over the galaxy’s core to take spectroscopic data — and right time — being at lower redshift. To get as broad a view of the spiral galaxy as possible across the electromagnetic spectrum, the team used Hubble’s ultraviolet- and Webb’s infrared-imaging and spectroscopic archival data, respectively.

“Because the Saguaro is at lower redshift, we can see the very beautiful and bright host galaxy in high resolution and detail with Webb and Hubble,” said Zihao Wu of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and a co-author of the study. “Webb’s observations can help us understand how the galaxy and its little red dot-like nucleus are connected.”

The team took multiple approaches to verify that the Saguaro’s compact red nucleus matched the characteristics of a prototypical LRD. In particular, the Hubble and Webb data showed that the nucleus is brighter in both ultraviolet and infrared light than in visible light, just like distant LRDs. The team also carefully disentangled the light emitted from the host and nucleus, and considered the presence of X-ray emission from the source.

Although the majority of little red dots at high redshift are not detectable in X-ray light, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory detected weak X-ray emission from the Saguaro.

“What the X-ray light observations show is that this galaxy has an active galactic nucleus, and a very obscured one at that,” said Carys Gilbert, a Master’s student at the University of Cape Town in South Africa and a co-author of the paper. “It’s not only obscured but also X-ray weak. That kind of combination could explain the lack of X-ray emission that we see from all other little red dots. It fits the puzzle of little red dots nicely.”

In addition to demonstrating how the Saguaro’s central compact red source fits the little red dot criteria, the team synthetically shifted the galaxy to a higher redshift to explore how this galactic environment would appear to observers if located in the early universe. As expected, the Saguaro’s surrounding galactic structure fades so that only the bright, LRD-like source at its center is visible.

“Our theory is that most of these distant sources are affected by this cosmological effect, creating an observational bias,” said Rinaldi. “We simply are not able to sample the immediate environment of high-redshift little red dots because their surroundings are just too faint to be observed even with Webb. Little red dots are far more complex than just being a dot. They’re just the tip of the iceberg — of a supermassive black hole interacting with its nearby surroundings.”

Image: Little Red Dot at Redshift 2: Real and Simulated Graphic

Scientists synthetically shifted the Saguaro, a lower-redshift spiral galaxy, to a higher redshift to find out how it would appear if it was in the early universe. Its compact red appearance suggests that little red dots are a phase of highly active supermassive black holes. Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, Pierluigi Rinaldi (Steward Observatory); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI); Illustration: Leah Hustak (STScI)

Considering the Saguaro case study, the team believes that LRDs may not be a unique galaxy population, but instead a temporary phase of highly active supermassive black holes. Could this theory be the link between the populous high-redshift little red dots seen by Webb and the local universe?

While the Saguaro is not representative of all LRDs, the team proposes that this is one phase of these compact red sources. To build more confidence, further study of the Saguaro is necessary, as well as seeking other Saguaro-like galaxies at lower redshift. The team also intends to comb through Webb’s bountiful archival data to build a census of little red dots to study how their environments may impact how they mature. These different approaches are all geared to helping uncover the family tree of little red dots.

The James Webb Space Telescope is the world’s premier space science observatory. Webb is solving mysteries in our solar system, looking beyond to distant worlds around other stars, and probing the mysterious structures and origins of our universe and our place in it. Webb is an international program led by NASA with its partners, ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for over three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA.

To learn more about Webb, visit:

https://science.nasa.gov/webb

To learn more about Hubble, visit:

https://science.nasa.gov/hubble

articles.personality_title: NASA Webb Telescope Reveals Life Cycle of Mysterious Cosmic Red Dots
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Since 2022, NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has spotted tiny red spots in space called little red dots (LRDs). These dots are very far away and hard to understand. Scientists thought they might be supermassive black holes, but their exact nature was unclear.

**What happened** – A team of researchers studied a spiral galaxy named “Saguaro” that has a small red center similar to the LRDs. By using images and data from Webb and the older Hubble Space Telescope, they learned that these red dots could be a temporary stage in the life of supermassive black holes. The Saguaro galaxy, about 3.3 billion years after the Big Bang, showed signs of a hidden, active black hole at its center.

**Impact** – This discovery helps explain why LRDs appear so often in the early universe but seem to disappear later. The team found that the faint surroundings of these dots are hard to see when they are very far away, making them look like just tiny red spots. This means LRDs are not unique objects but part of larger galaxies with active black holes. It changes how scientists understand the growth and evolution of black holes and galaxies.

**What's next step** – The researchers plan to study more galaxies like the Saguaro to confirm their findings. They will also search through Webb’s data to find more LRDs and learn how their environments affect their development. This will help build a clearer picture of how these mysterious cosmic dots evolve over time.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using Webb and Hubble data, scientists discovered that little red dots are a temporary phase of active supermassive black holes hidden in galaxies, solving a cosmic mystery about their nature and evolution.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le télescope Webb de la NASA révèle le cycle de vie des mystérieux points rouges cosmiques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis 2022, le télescope spatial James Webb de la NASA a détecté de petits points rouges dans l’espace appelés petits points rouges (LRD). Ces points sont très éloignés et difficiles à comprendre. Les scientifiques pensaient qu’ils pouvaient être des trous noirs supermassifs, mais leur nature exacte restait inconnue.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de chercheurs a étudié une galaxie spirale nommée « Saguaro » qui possède un petit centre rouge similaire aux LRD. En utilisant les images et données de Webb et du plus ancien télescope Hubble, ils ont découvert que ces points rouges pourraient être une étape temporaire dans la vie des trous noirs supermassifs. La galaxie Saguaro, datant d’environ 3,3 milliards d’années après le Big Bang, montre des signes d’un trou noir actif caché en son centre.

**Impact** – Cette découverte aide à comprendre pourquoi les LRD apparaissent souvent dans l’univers jeune mais semblent disparaître plus tard. L’équipe a trouvé que l’environnement faible autour de ces points est difficile à voir à grande distance, ce qui les fait paraître comme de simples petits points rouges. Cela signifie que les LRD ne sont pas des objets uniques mais font partie de galaxies plus grandes avec des trous noirs actifs. Cela change la façon dont les scientifiques comprennent la croissance et l’évolution des trous noirs et des galaxies.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs prévoient d’étudier davantage de galaxies comme la Saguaro pour confirmer leurs résultats. Ils chercheront aussi dans les données de Webb d’autres LRD afin de comprendre comment leur environnement influence leur développement. Cela permettra de mieux comprendre l’évolution de ces points rouges mystérieux.

**Une phrase clé** – Grâce aux données de Webb et Hubble, les scientifiques ont découvert que les petits points rouges sont une phase temporaire de trous noirs supermassifs actifs cachés dans des galaxies, résolvant un mystère cosmique sur leur nature et leur évolution.
articles.personality_title_es: El telescopio Webb de la NASA revela el ciclo de vida de los misteriosos puntos rojos cósmicos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Desde 2022, el telescopio espacial James Webb de la NASA ha detectado pequeños puntos rojos en el espacio llamados pequeños puntos rojos (LRD). Estos puntos están muy lejos y son difíciles de entender. Los científicos pensaban que podían ser agujeros negros supermasivos, pero su naturaleza exacta era desconocida.

Usando imágenes y datos de Webb y del más antiguo telescopio Hubble, aprendieron que estos puntos rojos podrían ser una etapa temporal en la vida de agujeros negros supermasivos. La galaxia Saguaro, que existe aproximadamente 3.3 mil millones de años después del Big Bang, mostró señales de un agujero negro activo y oculto en su centro.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento ayuda a explicar por qué los LRD aparecen con frecuencia en el universo temprano pero parecen desaparecer después. El equipo encontró que los alrededores tenues de estos puntos son difíciles de ver a grandes distancias, haciendo que parezcan solo pequeños puntos rojos. Esto significa que los LRD no son objetos únicos, sino parte de galaxias más grandes con agujeros negros activos. Cambia cómo los científicos entienden el crecimiento y evolución de agujeros negros y galaxias.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores planean estudiar más galaxias como la Saguaro para confirmar sus hallazgos. También buscarán en los datos de Webb más LRD para aprender cómo su entorno afecta su desarrollo. Esto ayudará a construir una imagen más clara de cómo evolucionan estos misteriosos puntos cósmicos.

**Una frase para llevar** – Usando datos de Webb y Hubble, los científicos descubrieron que los pequeños puntos rojos son una fase temporal de agujeros negros supermasivos activos ocultos en galaxias, resolviendo un misterio cósmico sobre su naturaleza y evolución.

articles.title: The search for life on Jupiter's icy moon Europa just got more complicated
articles.summary: Europa’s hidden ocean has made the icy moon one of the solar system’s most promising places to search for habitable conditions. Scientists have hoped that water from this deep ocean might rise through cracks and form shallow reservoirs that future spacecraft could more easily study. New simulations suggest that journey is unlikely because turbulent water would rapidly lose heat, form ice crystals, and clog the fractures, sometimes within hours.
articles.content:
Europa has captivated scientists for decades because a vast ocean of liquid water may be concealed beneath its frozen surface.

That buried sea has made Jupiter's icy moon one of the most promising places in the solar system to investigate whether conditions suitable for life might exist beyond Earth. However, new research led by Rutgers scientist Lujendra Ojha indicates that reaching material from Europa's deep ocean may be much more difficult than previously believed.

Testing a Possible Route Through Europa's Ice

In a study published in Nature Astronomy, Ojha and his colleagues used computer simulations to examine whether water from Europa's global ocean could travel upward through fractures in the ice and accumulate in shallow underground reservoirs. If such pockets exist, future spacecraft could potentially detect or sample them more easily than the ocean far below.

"The mystery we wanted to solve was whether this journey is actually possible," said Ojha, an associate professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at the Rutgers School of Arts and Sciences. "Can liquid water rise from Europa's deep ocean toward the surface without freezing along the way?"

The results suggest that the trip from the deep ocean into the upper layers of ice is far less likely than many scientists have assumed.

"There's an icy shell, there's water underneath, and there's all this speculation about how that water can come from deep underground and make its way all the way up without freezing en route," Ojha said. "That's really what we think we disproved."

Shallow Water May Have a Different Source

The conclusion could significantly affect how scientists interpret future discoveries on Europa. If spacecraft detect shallow pockets of liquid water beneath the surface, those reservoirs may not contain water that originated in the moon's deep ocean. They could instead have formed when sections of the ice shell melted locally.

The difference is important because scientists are drawn to Europa by the combination of liquid water, chemistry and energy, which are all essential factors when evaluating whether an environment could support life. Shallow water would be far easier to investigate than the deeply buried ocean. But if those reservoirs are isolated from the ocean, they may offer little information about Europa's most scientifically compelling environment.

Europa Clipper and JUICE Approach Jupiter

The findings come as two major missions travel toward the Jupiter system. NASA's Europa Clipper mission launched in October 2024 and is expected to reach Jupiter in April 2030. It will orbit the planet and complete 49 close flybys of Europa. The European Space Agency's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer mission, known as JUICE, launched in April 2023 and is scheduled to arrive at Jupiter in July 2031.

Together, the spacecraft are expected to provide a much clearer picture of Europa's frozen shell, surface chemistry and potential subsurface water. Radar aboard Europa Clipper may help researchers determine whether shallow reservoirs are present and reveal their size and structure.

Far below Europa's bitterly cold exterior, a global ocean may remain liquid because Jupiter's immense gravitational pull repeatedly stretches and compresses the moon. That motion produces internal heat, which becomes trapped beneath the thick ice shell.

Could Water Rise Through Fractures?

The new study examined dikes, which are narrow fractures that could theoretically serve as channels for ocean water moving upward through the ice. The concept loosely resembles the way molten rock travels through cracks in Earth's crust before contributing to volcanic eruptions. On frozen worlds, similar activity involving water and ice rather than molten rock is called cryovolcanism.

Ojha cautioned that the comparison between the two processes has clear limits.

"Ice and liquid water are fundamentally different than lava and the volcanoes that we see here on Earth," he said. "I think there's some fundamental physics that's missing here, and so I wanted to explore that."

One factor that previous models may have underestimated is turbulence. Earlier simulations often assumed that water would rise through Europa's ice in a relatively smooth and organized flow. The Rutgers-led research instead suggests that the water would move rapidly and chaotically, repeatedly mixing against the cold walls of the fracture and quickly transferring its heat into the surrounding ice.

"This water that's going to come up, it's going to be turbulent," Ojha said. "It's going to be left and right, it's going to be up and down, it's going to have a swirling motion. And when that happens, that liquid water is going to cool very, very fast as it approaches the surface."

Ice Crystals Could Clog the Path

As the rising water loses heat, it may become supercooled, remaining liquid even after its temperature falls below the normal freezing point. In that state, small crystals known as frazil ice can begin to form. Over time, those crystals may accumulate and block the fracture.

According to the simulations, narrow cracks could freeze closed in a matter of hours. Larger fractures might transport more water under ideal conditions, but turbulence makes even those situations much less favorable. The team found that moving enough water to create some of Europa's visible surface features would require fractures that are unrealistically long or present in unusually large numbers.

The findings point to a version of Europa in which any shallow liquid water may have formed separately from the global ocean. Rather than traveling upward from great depths, it may have been produced when localized heat melted portions of the ice shell.

"Our work suggests that Europa's ice shell may be a stronger barrier between the ocean and the surface than previously assumed," Ojha said. "This helps future missions interpret what they find and better understand where to look for signs of habitability."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific advancement in understanding Europa's ice shell and the challenges of detecting its subsurface ocean, which is crucial for assessing habitability and the search for extraterrestrial life. This research provides meaningful context for upcoming major space missions (Europa Clipper and JUICE) that have broad public and scientific interest. The detailed simulations and findings enhance our knowledge of planetary science and guide future exploration strategies, representing a positive step in space exploration and astrobiology.
articles.personality_title: New study reveals challenges in accessing Europa’s hidden ocean
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Europa, one of Jupiter’s moons, is covered by a thick shell of ice hiding a vast ocean beneath. Scientists believe this ocean could have conditions suitable for life, making Europa a key target for future space missions.

**What happened** – Researchers led by Lujendra Ojha at Rutgers University used computer simulations to test if water from Europa’s deep ocean can travel up through cracks in the ice to form pockets closer to the surface. Their results show that turbulent water would cool quickly, freeze, and block these cracks, making it very unlikely for ocean water to rise this way.

**Impact** – This means shallow pockets of water found near the surface may not come from the deep ocean but rather from local melting of the ice. Since the deep ocean is where conditions might support life, this finding changes how scientists will interpret data from upcoming missions like NASA’s Europa Clipper and ESA’s JUICE.

**What’s next step** – The Europa Clipper and JUICE spacecraft will arrive at Jupiter in the early 2030s. They will study Europa’s ice and surface in detail, helping to find and understand any shallow water pockets and better focus the search for signs of life.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New research shows Europa’s icy shell is a stronger barrier than thought, making it harder for ocean water to reach the surface and guiding future missions in the search for life.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude révèle les défis pour accéder à l’océan caché d’Europe
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Europe, l’une des lunes de Jupiter, est recouverte d’une épaisse couche de glace cachant un vaste océan en dessous. Les scientifiques pensent que cet océan pourrait avoir des conditions favorables à la vie, ce qui fait d’Europe une cible clé pour les futures missions spatiales.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs dirigés par Lujendra Ojha de l’Université Rutgers ont utilisé des simulations informatiques pour tester si l’eau de l’océan profond d’Europe peut remonter à travers des fissures dans la glace pour former des poches plus proches de la surface. Leurs résultats montrent que l’eau turbulente refroidirait rapidement, gèlerait et bloquerait ces fissures, rendant très peu probable la montée de l’eau océanique.

**Impact** – Cela signifie que les poches d’eau peu profondes trouvées près de la surface ne proviennent peut-être pas de l’océan profond, mais plutôt de la fonte locale de la glace. Comme l’océan profond est l’endroit où les conditions pourraient supporter la vie, cette découverte change la façon dont les scientifiques interpréteront les données des missions à venir comme Europa Clipper de la NASA et JUICE de l’ESA.

**Prochaine étape** – Les engins spatiaux Europa Clipper et JUICE arriveront à Jupiter au début des années 2030. Ils étudieront en détail la glace et la surface d’Europe, aidant à trouver et comprendre les poches d’eau peu profondes et à mieux cibler la recherche de signes de vie.

**Une phrase clé** – Une nouvelle recherche montre que la couche de glace d’Europe est une barrière plus forte que prévu, rendant plus difficile pour l’eau océanique d’atteindre la surface et guidant les futures missions dans la recherche de la vie.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio revela desafíos para acceder al océano oculto de Europa
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Europa, una de las lunas de Júpiter, está cubierta por una gruesa capa de hielo que oculta un vasto océano debajo. Los científicos creen que este océano podría tener condiciones adecuadas para la vida, convirtiendo a Europa en un objetivo clave para futuras misiones espaciales.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores liderados por Lujendra Ojha de la Universidad de Rutgers usaron simulaciones por computadora para probar si el agua del océano profundo de Europa puede subir por grietas en el hielo y formar bolsas más cerca de la superficie. Sus resultados muestran que el agua turbulenta se enfría rápido, se congela y bloquea estas grietas, haciendo muy poco probable que el agua del océano suba de esa forma.

**Impacto** – Esto significa que las bolsas de agua poco profundas cerca de la superficie pueden no venir del océano profundo, sino de derretimiento local del hielo. Como el océano profundo es donde podrían existir condiciones para la vida, este hallazgo cambia cómo los científicos interpretarán los datos de las próximas misiones como Europa Clipper de la NASA y JUICE de la ESA.

**Próximo paso** – Las naves Europa Clipper y JUICE llegarán a Júpiter a principios de la década de 2030. Estudiarán en detalle el hielo y la superficie de Europa, ayudando a encontrar y entender las bolsas de agua poco profundas y a enfocar mejor la búsqueda de señales de vida.

**Resumen en una frase** – Nueva investigación muestra que la capa de hielo de Europa es una barrera más fuerte de lo pensado, dificultando que el agua del océano llegue a la superficie y guiando futuras misiones en la búsqueda de vida.
